segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they came to the other side of the sea, to the region of the Gerasenes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he got out of the boat, at once a man with an unclean spirit came from the tombs to meet him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He had his dwelling among the tombs, and no one could bind him any longer, not even with a chain,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because he had often been bound with shackles and chains, and he had torn the chains apart and smashed the shackles, and no one was strong enough to subdue him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Constantly, night and day, among the tombs and in the hills, he was crying out and gashing himself with stones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Seeing Jesus from a distance, he ran and bowed down before him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and crying out in a loud voice he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What do you want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I put you under oath by God: do not torment me!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he had been saying to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he asked him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What is your name?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Legion is my name, for we are many.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the region.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they begged him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Send us into the pigs, so that we may enter them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he gave them permission. The unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs, and the herd, about two thousand of them, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and were drowned in the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who had been tending them fled and reported it in the town and in the countryside, and people came to see what it was that had happened.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, the very man who had had the legion, and they were afraid.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man, and told them about the pigs.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they began to beg him to leave their territory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been demon-possessed begged him that he might be with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He did not let him, but said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go home to your own people and report to them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a large crowd gathered around him, and he was beside the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of the synagogue leaders, named Jairus, came, and on seeing him fell at his feet

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and begged him earnestly, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he went with him. A large crowd was following him and pressing in on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now there was a woman who had had a flow of blood for twelve years.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She had suffered much under many doctors and had spent everything she had, and she was no better but had instead grown worse.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having heard about Jesus, she came up behind him in the crowd and touched his cloak,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for she had been saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If I touch even his clothes, I will be made well.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And at once the source of her bleeding dried up, and she knew in her body that she had been healed of her affliction.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And at once Jesus, aware in himself that power had gone out from him, turned around in the crowd and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Who touched my clothes?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “You see the crowd pressing in on you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he kept looking around to see the woman who had done this.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the woman, frightened and trembling, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell down before him and told him the whole truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be healthy, free of your affliction.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was still speaking, people came from the synagogue leader’s house, saying,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “Your daughter has died. Why trouble the teacher any further?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus, disregarding what was being said, told the synagogue leader,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not be afraid; only believe.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he did not let anyone accompany him except Peter, James, and John the brother of James.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to the synagogue leader’s house, and he saw a commotion, with people weeping and wailing loudly,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and going in he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child has not died but is sleeping.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they laughed at him. But he put them all out, took the child’s father and mother and those who were with him, and went in where the child was.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Taking the child by the hand, he said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Talitha koum,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which is translated,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Girl, I say to you, get up.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And at once the girl stood up and began walking around, for she was twelve years old. And at once they were overcome with great amazement.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He gave them strict orders that no one should know of this, and said that she should be given something to eat.

notes.note: Manuscripts vary between Gerasenes, Gadarenes and Gergesenes, here and in the parallel accounts. Gerasenes has the best early support in Mark and is the reading of the SBLGNT, but Gerasa (modern Jerash) lies more than thirty miles from the lake, which probably prompted copyists to substitute nearer places. The older English tradition, following later manuscripts, reads Gadarenes.

The verb describes the physical act of prostrating oneself before a superior, whether a god, a king or anyone whose power is acknowledged. Older versions have 'worshipped', which in modern English implies religious devotion. Here the act is the submission of a hostile spirit to a stronger power, so most recent translations also use 'bowed down' or 'fell on his knees'.

notes.phrase: I put you under oath by God
notes.note: The traditional 'adjure' is accurate but no longer ordinary English. The verb means to bind someone by an oath invoking a divine name, and it is the formula exorcists themselves used to command spirits (compare Acts 19:13). The irony is that here the spirit tries to use it on Jesus.

A Latin military term borrowed into Greek. A Roman legion at full strength numbered roughly five to six thousand soldiers, so the name signals an overwhelming occupying force as well as a great number. Whether Mark intends a political allusion to Roman occupation is debated.

In Jesus’s mouth 'the Lord' most naturally means God, as in the Septuagint. In the next verse, however, the man proclaims what 'Jesus' had done for him. Mark sets the two side by side without comment, and readers differ on how far he means to identify them.

The name means 'Ten Cities' and refers to a group of Hellenistic cities lying mostly east and south-east of the Sea of Galilee. The population was largely Gentile, which explains the presence of a large herd of pigs, animals unclean to Jews. This man is the first person in Mark to proclaim Jesus in Gentile territory.

The verb here and in verses 28 and 34 is the ordinary Greek word for rescuing from danger or illness, and is the same word rendered 'save' elsewhere in the New Testament. In a context of sickness a first-century reader would hear 'recover' or 'be cured', so it is rendered 'made well' in all three verses. Some translations have 'your faith has saved you' in verse 34, and Mark may intend the wider sense to be heard.

The phrase echoes the Septuagint wording of Leviticus 15, where a woman with a prolonged discharge of blood is ritually unclean, as is anything or anyone she touches. For twelve years the condition would have restricted her participation in ordinary religious and social life. This explains both her covert approach and her fear when discovered.

The verb can mean either 'overhear' or 'refuse to heed'. Most modern translations choose 'overhearing', and the parallel in Luke 8:50 has simply 'hearing'. The rendering here follows the sense the word has in the Septuagint and in its only other New Testament occurrence (Matthew 18:17). Either way, Jesus hears the message and refuses to let it stand.

Mark preserves Jesus’s words in Aramaic, the everyday language of Galilee, and then translates them for his Greek-speaking readers. The phrase means 'girl, get up'; 'I say to you' is added in Mark’s Greek translation. Many later manuscripts read 'koumi', the grammatically feminine form, which is the source of the traditional 'cumi'.
